candidates.source_name: EIA Today in Energy
candidates.snippet: What are crack spreads and why are they elevated? Crack spreads are indicators of the profitability of refining crude oil into petroleum products such as gasoline and diesel. One common crack spread is calculated by subtracting the spot market price of a gallon of crude oil from the wholesale price of a gallon of refined product. Since May, the gasoline crack spread in New York Harbor has averaged about $1 per gallon (gal) higher than in 2025, when the crack spread peaked around 60 cents/gal. Gasoline crack spreads are elevated primarily because of tight gasoline supplies globally.

US Marines board Iranian tanker in Gulf of Oman amid blockade enforcement
Author: Vinod Kumar (UAE)
US Marines board Iranian tanker in Gulf of Oman amid blockade enforcement
File photo/getty images
US Marines have boarded and redirected an Iranian-flagged commercial oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman, suspected of attempting to evade the US Navy blockade on Iranian shipping.
US Central Command identified the vessel as the M/T Celestial Sea, saying it was searched and forced to alter course after it appeared to be heading toward an Iranian port. It is at least the fifth vessel boarded since the Trump administration imposed the blockade earlier this year.
Central Command said US forces have now redirected 91 commercial ships to ensure compliance. Four vessels have been disabled since the blockade began on April 12. The boarding comes amid a tense diplomatic backdrop.
President Donald Trump recently called off renewed military strikes on Iran to allow room for negotiations – but enforcement at sea has shown no sign of easing.
Earlier this month, a US Navy fighter jet fired precision munitions at the smokestacks of two Iranian-flagged tankers that attempted to reach an Iranian port in defiance of the blockade.
On May 6, another aircraft fired on the tanker M/T Hasna in the Strait of Hormuz after it ignored repeated warnings.
US forces also destroyed six Iranian small boats launched by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps toward Navy vessels escorting ships through the strait.The blockade, in place since April 13, targets all vessels entering or leaving Iranian ports. The US says it is costing Iran 500 million dollars a day.
Iran has seized two cargo ships in retaliation.

candidates.source_name: LRASM and JASSM Production to Triple Under New Air Force Contract - Naval News
candidates.snippet:
Air Force targets a massive inventory boost of over 16,000 cruise missiles to shore up long-range stockpiles for potential Pacific contingencies.
Share
The U.S.
Air Force now anticipates buying more than 16,000 new JASSM and LRASM cruise missiles over the next five to seven years according to a notice of intent published Friday , dramatically expanding the Pentagon’s JASSM and LRASM topline inventory objectives for both weapons that have had their objectives periodically increased over the past decade.
The move comes amid a second contract modification to a LRASM/JASSM buy in 2024, increasing the topline number from 5,510 to 6,645.
The move comes amid large-scale reconstitution in the wake of Operation Epic Fury, as well as major demand signals from the Pentagon to push suppliers towards internal investments to support higher production rates of key weapons needed for a potential conflict in the Pacific.
The planned procurement would span JASSM Lots 27–33 and LRASM Lots 13–19, covering up to 16,450 missiles in multiple variants over the next five to seven years.
The contract covers all current and future variants of the LRASM and JASSM, including the new LRASM-ER and JASSM-XR — two new variants of the shared missile family that add some of Lockheed Martin’s newest anti-spoofing and survivability equipment.
U.S.
Air Force officials acknowledged that expanding production to support the larger procurement will require substantial upfront investment and an extended manufacturing ramp-up.
The notice also says government-owned production equipment remains committed to Lockheed Martin’s existing JASSM and LRASM contracts in the interim, supporting the company’s initiative to begin investing heavily into its supply chains and current production lines to meet new production demands.
These investments in facilities, tooling, suppliers and workforce are enabling higher production rates at speed and scale.”
Lockheed Martin spokesperson to Naval News A U.S. Air Force B-2A Spirit fires an AGM-158C LRASM towards a SINKEX target during Valiant Shield 2026, a joint force field training exercise designed to test the limits of U.S.
war strategy in the Pacific. (U.S. Air Force photo by Tech Sgt. Thomas Barley)
Lockheed Martin’s JASSM family has centered itself as the Pentagon’s major strike system for large-scale combat operations.
Pentagon planners continue to construct long-range acquisition forecasts around a notional major regional conflict in the Pacific, with both JASSM and LRASM in the forefront of nearly every major simulated conflict.
The planned buy in the U.S.
Air Force notice far exceeds publicly disclosed inventory objectives across both missile families, reflecting the Pentagon’s objective of scaling up production of its most critical weapons to wartime-adjacent levels.

Pentagon moves to triple Patriot, quadruple THAAD interceptor production
By Natalie Oliverio
Monday, Aug 3, 2026
U.S. Army soldiers remove a Terminal High Altitude Area Defense power generation unit during maintenance operations in the Middle East. (U.S. Army)
The Defense Department on Monday announced framework agreements with Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin aimed at expanding production of critical Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptor components as the military seeks to replenish missile inventories through expanded, long-term production capacity.
The agreements come as demand for Patriot and THAAD interceptors has increased following conflicts in Iran and Ukraine that strained U.S. missile inventories .
They also come days after a Center for Strategic and International Studies analysis estimated the United States had depleted roughly two-thirds of its pre-war Patriot interceptor inventory during the conflict with Iran.
Defense officials said the agreements are intended to support the department’s long-term procurement objective of nearly 14,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors by providing sustained demand signals to critical suppliers throughout the defense industrial base.
The initiative is designed to triple production capacity for Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors and quadruple production capacity for THAAD interceptors.
DoD said it will work directly with key component suppliers instead of relying solely on prime contractors, encouraging investment in advanced tooling, facility modernization and workforce development needed to sustain higher production rates.
“Building the Arsenal of Freedom requires robust, dynamic supply chains at every level of the industrial base,” Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in a statement.
“Framework agreements with munition components suppliers like Northrop Grumman are vital to accelerating the tripling of PAC-3 and quadrupling of THAAD interceptor production.”
The agreements establish a second source for Patriot solid rocket motors, expand production of ignition safety devices for PAC-3 interceptors and increase manufacturing capacity for key THAAD structural components, including mid-body shells, muzzle covers and rail car assemblies.
The initiative is part of the Defense Department’s Acquisition Transformation Strategy and was developed in coordination with the Missile Defense Agency, the Munitions Acceleration Council and the Economic Defense Unit to strengthen the resilience of the missile production supply chain.

L3Harris Technologies is planning a $1.27 billion expansion of its manufacturing site in Orange County, Virginia, to bolster its production of solid rocket motors for the Department of Defense.

“The company’s ongoing investments in new facilities, equipment and processes will enable it to double, triple and quadruple solid rocket motor production rates for a range of key programs,” L3Harris said in a release .

The TNT choke point
Trinitrotoluene, or TNT as it’s more commonly known, is a chemical compound central to the production of modern munitions used in artillery shells, aerial bombs, and mines.
While NATO has focused much of its recent effort on expanding final ammunition assembly, access to explosives like TNT has emerged as a quieter but critical constraint.
Some reports and industry estimates have put Russia’s explosives output at a level equivalent to around 50,000 tonnes of TNT per year, which is orders of magnitude above what Europe can reliably source at home.
Europe effectively has a single NATO-standard TNT producer: Nitro-Chem in Poland, a facility where TNT production dates back to 1948.
Public reporting has pegged the plant’s capacity at up to 12,000 tonnes per year, with a significant share already committed under long-term contracts, including supplies to the United States — leaving European manufacturers dependent on imports from Asia to make up the shortfall.
Swebal, for its part, has spent the past 14 months since its inception laying the groundwork — from permitting and early engineering to initial fundraising — to bring new TNT capacity online in Sweden.
“One of the major bottlenecks of increasing production rates of large-caliber ammunition, was the access to explosives, which brings us to where we are today – attacking a bottleneck to make Europe a safer place to live,” Sjöblom said.
To date, Swebal has raised €3 million ($3.5 million) in early-stage funding from a group of private investors that includes EQT co-founder Thomas von Koch , former Swedish army chief Karl Engelbrektson , and Pär Svärdson , founder of online pharmacy Apotea. The company is using the capital to address that bottleneck at industrial scale.
To start with, Swebal is targeting an annual output of up to 4,500 tonnes of TNT by 2028, a level Sjöblom describes as a balance between Europe’s near-term needs and what can realistically be financed and absorbed by the market.
“The long-term volume requirements are hard to forecast,” he said.
“We ended up with a production capacity that is the balance of what is commercially feasible to sell, where we can confirm the requirements, and with a related capital investment that can be funded on sustainable terms. Hopefully, we can repurpose any future positive cash flow to contribute even more to Europe’s defense.”
Once operational, the facility is expected to run around the clock, using a production process known as “continuous nitration.” Swebal says the plant will employ roughly 50 people, while much of the required materials and equipment are expected to be sourced within a radius of around 550 kilometres, concentrating the supply chain around the Baltic
A race to rebuild
Much of the recent surge in activity has focused on defence technology — software, sensors, and systems — rather than the heavy industrial manufacturing required to produce energetics (e.g. explosives and propellants) and ammunition at scale.

For private credit borrowers, big maturity walls are further out
May 1 (Reuters) - For most companies that have borrowed from U.S. private credit funds, the real moment of reckoning - when their loans mature and they need to refinance cheap ​debt taken during the COVID-19 pandemic years - is a couple of years ‌away.
A Reuters analysis of U.S.
Securities and Exchange Commission filings from 74 private credit funds, also known as business development companies (BDCs), found only about $15 billion of a total $84 billion of their assets mature ​this year, with the bulk of loan maturities peaking in 2028 and 2029.

The ​data allays some fears in the private banking sector facing strains ⁠from higher interest rates, weaker earnings growth and pressure on profitability in the software ​sector.
Shares of BDCs, which are private investment funds that lend directly to many mid-sized borrowers, ​have been under pressure and faced redemptions due to these concerns.
Shows BDC loan maturities fall between 2026-2029
Lotfi Karoui, multi-asset credit strategist at bond fund manager PIMCO, said in a note the amount of upcoming debt due for refinancing for ​software borrowers in the leveraged loan and direct lending markets also appeared modest.
"The good ​news is that relatively benign near-term refinancing needs for software companies limit the risk of an abrupt ‌rise ⁠in financial distress," he said in a recent note.
Shows debt maturity schedule for BDC companies
Credit quality in BDC loan portfolios is weakening, with non-accruals rising and payment-in-kind income increasing in parts of the sector, according to a Fitch Ratings report.
Companies with loans maturing this year could face refinancing pressure, forcing ​them to seek more ​amend-and-extend transactions, which ⁠push out repayment dates by changing loan terms, as well as repricings and other liability-management exercises.
Software and technology borrowers are among those ​drawing scrutiny from investors, given slower growth and concerns about ​AI disruption.
The ⁠risks could be amplified for loans overlapping BDC portfolios, since stress at any one borrower with multiple creditors could pressure loan valuations and net asset value (NAV) across the sector.
For BDCs whose ⁠shares ​are already trading at a discount to NAV, that ​could make it harder to raise equity without diluting shareholders' interest and could increase their cost of capital.

Riskier loan issuers push back maturity wall via amend-and-extend deals
These deals, which allow issuers to push out loan maturities without refinancing into a new credit, are printing at a record clip.
| By Richard Kellerhals

The $21.2 billion of amend-and-extend leveraged loan dealmaking in December was the fourth consecutive month of greater than $20 billion, capping a record year.
The total for 2024 was $226 billion, easily eclipsing the previous record set in 2023 of $176 billion.
For reference, amend-and-extend transactions allow issuers to push out loan maturities without refinancing into a new credit, which would require marking the entire loan to market and could entail higher spreads, a new OID, etc.
In return, lenders typically receive a higher applicable margin on their extended loans and may receive additional compensation, including extension or amendment fees.
The record pace of A&E deals is particularly noteworthy in the current climate, as the average yield to maturity for refinancing institutional term loans via syndication in 2023 was 9.6%, a 23-year high. That average was down slightly, at 8.6% in 2024, still up significantly from historical averages.
December’s amend-and-extend activity came courtesy of 25 transactions, with institutional deals dominating volumes at $12.1 billion versus the $9.1 billion from the pro rata side.
This was driven by a massive repricing wave that is washing over the institutional loan market, with almost 100 repricing transactions closing last month alone — and many of those repricing transactions come alongside extensions.
The prevalence of institutional amend-and-extend transactions was a departure from the past few years, when the pro rata market supplied the majority of A-and-E activity.
Sponsored amend-and-extend transactions ran just ahead of non-sponsored activity in 2023, but non-sponsored deals edged to the front in 2024, with a 53% share.
Meanwhile, sponsored and non-sponsored companies with pro rata loans mostly chipped away at 2026 maturities through the end of 2024 — extending $52.7 billion of debt due that year — along with $38.2 billion due in 2027 and $19.7 billion due in 2025.
On the institutional side, activity has been focused on 2027 and 2028 maturities, with borrowers extending $32 billion and $40.6 billion coming due in those years, respectively, although $22.7 billion of institutional loans coming due in 2026 were also extended.
For context, the amount outstanding in the leveraged loan market as referenced by the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index was $1.4 trillion at the end of 2024. Loan volume maturing through the end of 2025 has narrowed to $15.8 billion at the end of 2024, from $81.3 billion at the end of 2023.

For reference, amend-and-extend transactions allow issuers to push out loan maturities without refinancing into a new credit, which would require marking the entire loan to market and could entail higher spreads, a new OID, etc.
In return, lenders typically receive a higher applicable margin on their extended loans and may receive additional compensation, including extension or amendment fees.
This record pace of A&E deals is particularly noteworthy in the current climate, as the average yield-to-maturity for refinancing institutional term loans via syndication in 2023 was 9.6%, a 23-year high. That average is down slightly, at 9.2% so far this year, but is still significantly above historical averages.
April’s amend-and-extend activity came courtesy of 24 borrowers, near January’s record tally of 26. Activity was almost evenly split between institutional and pro rata executions, with $7.2 billion recorded on the institutional side and $7.3 billion recorded on the pro rata side.
The steady supply of institutional amend-and-extend transactions has been quite a departure from the average over the past two years, when the pro rata market dominated monthly activity. This departure can also be connected to the rise in sponsored versus non-sponsored amend-and-extend transactions.
Notable transactions on the institutional side included Global Medical Response’s extended $3.57 billion first-lien term loan and DaVita’s extended $1.64 billion term loan B-1 .
On the pro rata side, notable transactions included Chart Industries’ extension of its upsized $1.25 billion revolver , Crescent Energy’s extension of its $1.7 billion revolver and Vail Resorts’ extension of its pro rata facility , which consists of a $984 million term loan A and a $500 million revolver.
Pro rata debt typically entails amortizing TLAs and/or revolving credit facilities and is traditionally syndicated to finance companies and banks. Institutional debt consists of term loans structured specifically for institutional investors, including CLOs.
While there is heightened urgency to address near-term maturities, LCD data show that companies being given breathing room are, by and large, not immediate default candidates. Roughly 84% of the amendments completed in the year to date from this analysis are rated B-minus or higher at the issuer level, versus 82% in 2023 and 77% in 2022.
Maturity wall The amount outstanding in the leveraged loan market as referenced by the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index was $1.4 trillion at the end of April. Despite that wall of debt, borrowers have secured some breathing room.

Amend-and-extend volume rose to $16.1 billion in July, from $15.4 billion in June, according to LCD. While the monthly pace has held steady, overall activity remains subdued compared with recent years.
Year-to-date volume stands at $99 billion, well below the $133 billion recorded over the same period in 2024.
It’s unclear to what extent broader market volatility has impacted US leveraged loan issuers’ ability to refresh their credit facilities.
Note that both 2023 and 2024 set all-time A&E records, with 2024 surpassing the prior year by a wide margin.
For reference, amend-and-extend transactions allow issuers to push out loan maturities without refinancing into a new credit, which would require marking the entire loan to market and could entail higher spreads, a new OID, etc.
In return, lenders typically receive a higher applicable margin on the extended loans and may receive additional compensation, including extension or amendment fees.
The average yield to maturity for refinancing institutional term loans via syndication is 7.6% in 2025, down from 8.6% in 2024 and 9.6% in 2023, but still elevated from levels in 2009–2022.
July’s A&E mix shifted notably toward institutional loans, which accounted for $11.2 billion of the month’s total, versus $4.9 billion in pro rata volume.
So far this year, borrowers have extended $20.5 billion of pro rata facilities due in 2026, $21.5 billion due in 2027 and $7.7 billion due in 2028.
Institutional borrowers in 2024 focused on 2027 and 2028 maturities ($32 billion each), though they also extended $22.7 billion of institutional loans due in 2026.
This year, borrowers have extended $5.2 billion of institutional facilities due in 2027 and $28.1 billion due in 2028.
For context, the amount outstanding in the leveraged loan market per the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index was $1.49 trillion at the end of July.
Meanwhile, LCD reported five covenant-relief transactions in July, matching May and June levels, for a year-to-date total of 24. There were 21 transactions for the same period in 2024.
Of course, one of the fundamental differences in the covenant-relief landscape today is that the overwhelming majority of current covenant-relief deals are pro rata.
Note that because the vast majority of the outstanding US leveraged loans are covenant-lite (and pro rata deals are required to have covenants), it stands to reason that most of today’s covenant-relief activity is for pro rata deals.
